item.title: Why Compensation Doesn’t Foster Engagement
item.description:
Career

Why Compensation Doesn’t Foster Engagement

Why financially worthwhile work isn’t always psychologically engaging.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Total compensation can reduce dissatisfaction without creating work engagement.
  • Retaining employees, though, isn’t the same thing as psychologically engaging them.
  • Work engagement reflects psychological investment in the work itself, not just satisfaction.
  • Compensation may make work more tolerable without making it genuinely engaging.
Source: AI-generated; OpenAI/ChatGPT 5.5

I recently came across an HR Dive piece by Megan Ewen discussing a new report suggesting that total compensation—which includes salary, benefits, bonuses, and other financial incentives tied to employment—may not be enough to drive employee engagement.

My immediate reaction was: Of course it isn’t. But then I got to thinking that if organizations and consulting firms are treating the weak connection between compensation and engagement as a meaningful insight, maybe my reaction wasn’t as self-evident as I initially assumed.

Still, the reason for my reaction here is not exactly groundbreaking. It goes back, at least in part, to a distinction a guy named Frederick Herzberg made in the late 1950s.

The Two-Factor Theory of Work Motivation

In 1959, Frederick Herzberg (and his colleagues) published a book where they laid out what became known as the two-factor theory of work motivation. The central idea was that the factors that create dissatisfaction at work are not necessarily the same factors that create motivation or psychological investment in the work itself.

Herzberg referred to the first category as hygiene factors. These included things like salary, benefits, job security, organizational policies, and working conditions—essentially many of the external conditions surrounding the job itself. According to Herzberg, these factors mattered because when they were inadequate, employees became dissatisfied. But improving them didn’t necessarily create enthusiasm for the work itself. Instead, they primarily prevented dissatisfaction.

The second category involved what Herzberg called motivators—factors such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth, and meaningful work. These were more closely tied to intrinsic involvement in the work itself.

So, in more modern terms, hygiene factors are the kinds of things we often associate with job satisfaction—factors that help keep workers from leaving but that may have relatively little to do with actual work engagement. These factors matter, maybe even a great deal. But they’re often better at preventing dissatisfaction than creating psychological investment in the work itself.

That’s largely where total compensation falls. After all, there’s a meaningful difference between reducing dissatisfaction and creating genuine psychological investment in the work itself.

Why Work Engagement Isn’t a Function of Total Compensation

Total compensation is important. Organizations use it to attract and retain workers and to remain competitive in the labor market. Just like other contextual aspects of employment—supervision, organizational policies, workplace safety, flexibility, and the broader work environment—compensation matters because employees care about the conditions under which they work.

Workers, of course, also generally prefer employers that pay well and offer strong benefits packages. When compensation is perceived as inadequate or unfair, dissatisfaction is likely to increase, and workers may become more motivated to leave. But that's fundamentally different from being psychologically engaged in the work they perform. Compensation may influence whether employees want the job, but It doesn't determine whether they find the work itself meaningful, stimulating, or intrinsically rewarding once they arrive.

And that distinction is important because work engagement isn’t simply about liking one’s employer or feeling reasonably satisfied with employment conditions. Sure, those things matter, but work engagement reflects a deeper psychological connection to the work itself.

What Actually Creates Work Engagement?

Work engagement tends to emerge less from the conditions surrounding employment and more from employees' direct experience with the work they do. People are more likely to become psychologically invested in work when they experience some combination of autonomy, meaningfulness, challenge, growth, competence, and social connection. They want to feel that what they’re doing matters, they’re capable of doing it well, and they have at least some meaningful degree of control over how they do it.

And those things are psychologically different from compensation. A person can be very well compensated while simultaneously feeling bored, detached, emotionally exhausted, or disconnected from the work they perform each day. Likewise, someone can find work deeply meaningful and psychologically engaging while still feeling dissatisfied with their compensation. The two are certainly related, and they often correlate fairly strongly in organizational research. But they’re still not interchangeable.

Unfortunately, organizations often seem to treat engagement as something that can be engineered primarily through compensation adjustments, perks, incentives, wellness initiatives, and engagement campaigns while leaving the actual structure of work largely untouched. But if employees don't find the work itself meaningful, stimulating, appropriately challenging, or connected to a sense of growth and competence, increasing compensation alone is unlikely to suddenly create deep psychological investment in the work itself.

That doesn’t mean contextual factors—the category in which total compensation largely resides—are irrelevant. Poor supervision, unsafe work conditions, inadequate compensation, and dysfunctional organizational policies can absolutely undermine morale, increase dissatisfaction, and interfere with employees’ ability to fully engage in their work. But that still doesn’t make those factors synonymous with engagement itself.

In other words, organizations can often reduce dissatisfaction without necessarily creating engagement. An employee may appreciate a raise, feel satisfied with a strong benefits package, and have little interest in leaving the organization while still feeling only minimally connected to the actual work being performed each day.

In some ways, this broader dynamic also underlies at least some facets of the "quiet quitting" discourse.1 It wasn’t that employees were literally quitting. They continued showing up, performing their assigned responsibilities, and remaining employed. In many cases, they didn’t appear dissatisfied enough to leave their organizations. They may have appreciated their compensation, benefits, flexibility, or general employment stability. But they also often seemed to lack any deeper psychological investment in the work itself.

That shouldn’t be especially surprising. Work becomes difficult to engage with psychologically when employees experience it primarily as a series of fragmented or excessive demands that consume time and energy without creating much sense of meaning, growth, competence, or accomplishment in return. Under those conditions, compensation may make the situation more tolerable, but tolerance and engagement aren’t even in the same semantic zip code.

Engagement and the Nature of Work

Which brings me back to the original HR Dive article. The finding that total compensation is only weakly tied to work engagement is not especially surprising once we distinguish between factors that help attract and retain workers and factors that create genuine psychological investment in the work itself.

Compensation matters. Inadequate or unfair compensation can absolutely create dissatisfaction, undermine morale, and increase turnover risk. But making employment financially worthwhile is not the same thing as making work psychologically engaging.

And if organizations continue trying to address engagement primarily through contextual add-ons—compensation enhancements, perks, wellness initiatives, and similar interventions—while leaving the actual experience of work largely untouched, they’re likely to keep chasing their tails.2 After all, reducing dissatisfaction and creating genuine engagement in the work itself were never the same thing to begin with.

item.title: Philosophy Versus Logic-Chopping
item.description:
Philosophy

Philosophy Versus Logic-Chopping

A shared problem of online and analytic philosophy.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Much of analytic philosophy reduces philosophy to logic-chopping.
  • Vagueness is an inherent element of science itself.
  • To evaluate philosophical views objectively, we should discuss the theoretical merits of alternative views.

What is my least favourite genre of philosophy writing?

Philosophy Versus Logic-Chopping
Source: AI-generated with Chat-GPT / OpenAI

Many analytic philosophers despise the obscurantist, vague, and unclear writing style of continental philosophers, but at least that writing style can often be entertaining and occasionally deeply insightful. But as a philosopher working in the Anglosphere, continental philosophy isn’t something I encounter much anyhow. Analytic philosophy is the law of the land.

And so, as a naturalist philosopher, I find a particularly common style of writing and reasoning among analytic philosophers far more off-putting, given how frequently I encounter it.

It is also a style of writing that is common in online philosophy, where it’s all too common to try to debunk a position in a single comment, or dunk on a view with a single short argument, as if philosophical positions could be easily reduced to a short list of premises that can easily be dispelled.

Logic-Chopping in Analytic Philosophy

The problem I have with much of analytic philosophy is that it reduces philosophy to logic-chopping.

It is the kind of dry and over-precisified writing style aimed at objectivity, but that misses the forest for the trees—effectively ending up straw-manning most of the views it is trying to debunk.

If all you have available in your toolkit is an evaluation of whether a philosophical position is coherent or not, I am not very interested in what you have to say, since that is not very interesting at all. A great many philosophical articulations of theories may have logical inconsistencies, falling far short of offering deductive proof. But why care about debunking an incoherent version of an idea that can be made coherent?

Even as an atheist, I have little doubt that one could offer a logically coherent worldview that includes a God. It’s not that hard to add extra variables to a model. Even as a staunch materialist, I don’t doubt that someone could give a logically coherent account of panpsychism. I just don’t care much for the straw-manning of an entire position, declaring it logically incoherent because one might succeed at showing that one version of a theory is incoherent. Not to mention that many such philosophy articles, or blog posts for that matter, create a straw-man version of a view. Like Dan Dennett, I think we went too far in turning philosophy into mere logic-chopping:

I like to think I’m drifting back to what philosophy used to be, which has been forgotten in many quarters in philosophy during the last thirty or forty years, when philosophy has become a sometimes ridiculously technical and dry, logic-chopping subject for a lot of people — applied logic, applied mathematics. There’s always a place for that, but it’s nowhere near as big a place as a lot of people think. - Daniel C. Dennett

article continues after advertisement

Naturalist Approach

As a naturalist, I prefer to think about philosophical theories as just another species of scientific theory. Logical analysis, of course, does have a place in the sciences. But vagueness is an inherent element of science itself. Many of the attempts to debunk Darwin’s theory of evolution through dry logic-chopping amounted to little more than providing effective proof that logic-chopping isn’t all that conducive to evaluating whether we should endorse a theory or not. Even if a particular specification of a theory has inconsistent assumptions, these can easily be fixed. Pointing out such problems is no proof that an entire theory is misguided.

The same applies to conflicts between views like atheism versus theism. The scientific philosopher compares the various theoretical virtues of the best versions of alternative theories, which are all assumed to be capable of being made logically coherent. The geocentric model of the world was not discarded because it was logically incoherent, but because its theoretical virtues diminished compared to those of the heliocentric one.

Much of analytic philosophy has become entirely dry by restricting itself to uninteresting logic-chopping alone. The same goes for much philosophical argumentation online. While this approach may succeed in showing particular versions of views or particular authors to be mistaken, it adds little value to the grand scheme of evaluating the very best versions of theories we can and ought to articulate to make serious attempts at understanding reality.

Unfortunately, this much more important work does not easily lend itself to online comments, tweets, blog posts, or often enough even journal articles. The very architecture of our modern engagement with philosophy encourages logic-chopping and the straw-manning of positions, reducing philosophy to single arguments. As if one argument alone could undermine or prove a particular position… (sometimes it can, but don’t just confidently proclaim that your argument is the final nail in the coffin).

article continues after advertisement

Once we try to steel-man, rather than straw-man, philosophical or scientific theories, logic chopping has little value left to add, since we already work on the assumption that the best theories are logically coherent. But for some analytic philosophers, logic-chopping has unfortunately become their only tool of the trade. All in the hope that all theories but one will eventually show themselves to be incoherent.

But that is a vain hope indeed.

If we have to choose between a vision of philosophy as applied logic versus philosophy as abstract science, we should choose the latter—vastly expanding our toolbox to answer philosophical questions.

That’s why I consider myself a naturalist (scientific) philosopher. Not an analytic philosopher. (See this blog post.)

If you really want to convince someone to change their mind, or if you really want to evaluate alternative philosophical views in an objective manner, you should engage in a discussion about the theoretical merits of alternative views on the table. What are the trade-offs between them? What are the methods we should use to decide between these views? Don’t quibble about the details of how the views are articulated too much. There is a time and place for that, but let’s not miss the forest for the trees. Philosophy has much more to offer.

item.title: 'Mommy, I'm Bored': Summer Cries for Help
item.description:
Boredom

'Mommy, I'm Bored': Summer Cries for Help

Children can find it difficult on family trips away. What you can do about this.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • For some children, being with oneself, especially in an unfamiliar place, can be difficult.
  • Especially for children who are used to a lot of electronic stimulation, not having it can be very difficult.
  • Summer is a wonderful time for learning new ways of enjoying oneself and finding time for family togetherness.

“Mommy, I'm bored!” shouted 9-year-old Emily. “I have nothing to do, and no one will play with me,” she whined. Lori just didn't understand. For her, times at the beach in summer, especially alone times, were heavenly. And there were plenty of other children around in the neighborhood. If only Emily would venture out. If only she would give up her iPad and become involved with life by the water! If only…

Mark also was having difficulty. Not having grown up by the beach, he was used to long summer baseball practices, games, and hanging out with his teammates afterward. No matter how much he tried, fishing with his father-in-law just didn't cut it. Lori was starting to wish they had stayed home. She felt like she had two youngsters on her hands, and both of them were draining her with cries of "Mommy, I'm bored!"

We understand being bored as a state of mind in which emotion paralyzes curiosity and renders the individual trapped in ennui as long as they stay passive. It can happen for a child in school when feelings of being swamped, inadequate, or confused become connected with learning and overwhelm their ability to absorb what they are trying to learn. Negative feelings have stifled their curiosity about learning something new or figuring something out. It can happen socially when a child's feelings about being accepted can overwhelm their social confidence and leave them feeling outside a social group. Negative feelings here can paralyze their confidence, and they protectively withdraw, saying they don't like socializing. Then, alone, boredom sets in. It can happen on a beach where feelings of fear or of being dwarfed by nature can lead a child to feel unable to recognize the potential for fun in nature. Sand just feels itchy and can't turn into castles, water is too cold, and approaching other children feels daunting.

How Parents Can Help

To remedy this chain of self-defeating thoughts and behaviors, a parent has to be able to step outside of their own experience and accept that their child is having a hard time. Scolding will not lead to an improved circumstance. What can a parent do to help?

Becoming a playmate for a while is a good idea. It can remind a child of things to do, which leads to fun and a better mood. Your play may seem inviting to other children who want to join in, which can change your child's day. Similarly, it is also beneficial to support your bored spouse by encouraging them to join in an activity with you. Although you may feel like you have another child on your hands, this is best done with empathy; leave the spousal snarkiness behind.

The Impact of Technology and Screens on Imagination and Play

Through our observation of children, we have found that some easily slip into fantasy play and can make up scenarios that enrapture them. They become captivated by their own creativity. But we also have found that playing alone and in fantasy can be difficult for some children. Unfortunately, many children today have become so used to their screens—games, social media, videos—that they don't know how to find and create their own "entertainment" from within themselves. They need outside help to get something started. Show them how and what to do in play. They can learn. Often this involves setting limits on screen time for a child. Requiring them to do something they don't want to do, like giving up their screens for a while, is not easy for a parent or child. But this kind of limit-setting is an important part of parenting today. And it is necessary when you want to influence your child's activity. Many children can't make the switch on their own.

Summer is a wonderful time to try new activities and learn how to find entertainment and enjoyment in new ways. Think of your child's boredom not as a plague or something to fix but, rather, as an opportunity to help them develop new ways to enjoy themselves. Fantasy play and enactment are wonderful for children once they learn how to slip into their imaginations. Learning how to approach other children with a parent as a bridge is a gateway to new activities and friendships. Reading, playing games, and cooking with grandma all provide that, too. Gateways to being with oneself in new ways bring with them good feelings from the inside, feelings of self-reliance, accomplishment, creativity, and the excitement of exploration and developing interests.

It is important to note that if your child remains very resistant to your prompts and pushes, it could be that they have underlying anxiety or depressed feelings that leave them self-absorbed, inflexible, or guarded. You may even have had some comments about these tendencies from a teacher at school. It’s a good idea to pay attention to this and seek advice from your pediatrician.

We have found that many children who said they were bored, later, with a little parental assistance, will comment on how much they miss their vacation time away from routines and school. When a child actively moves past boredom into something fun, they feel good about it and good about themselves. Parents can be the best models. Most everyone can swap screen time for together time.

item.title: Integrating Military Life Skills Into Sports and Performance
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Integrating Military Life Skills Into Sports and Performance

Using breathing, composure, and decision-making processes to enable effectiveness.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Military training teaches life skills that work well beyond the battlefield into everyday living.
  • Slow, rhythmic breathing delivers composed presence, focus, and performance.
  • A calm voice communicates self-control and effective leadership, and brings composure to others.
Navy SEALs well-prepared for the challenges faced in the military context.
Source: Jeffrey Lowshaw / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

Warfare is what many people think of when reflecting on the military. That association can block the recognition of the life lessons that can be learned without ever serving in the armed forces.

Skills connected with military training can benefit all of us—including athletes and other performers—for dealing with the difficult, stressful circumstances we all encounter.

A few of those life lessons are explored herein. The link between military mental training and the approaches used in athletic and clinical psychology settings will be made, especially with Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT), a methodology used by performance psychology specialists to train military personnel and athletes.

Let’s get started.

Deliberate (Tactical) Breathing

Central to many military-trained skills is effective breathing.

Defined as slow, rhythmic breathing, deliberate (tactical) breathing is a skill trained for the maintenance of calm composure and the ability to be in the present moment. These are key components during stressful and life-threatening conditions experienced by the military.

Tactical breathing can also be of assistance for athletes. While sports may not be quite as dangerous as a military context, they can be stressful. Deliberate breathing can assist in not letting intense emotions obstruct the execution of the skills required for effective athletic performance. Such breathing is a central element of what ACT and other psychological approaches term mindfulness and allows for purposeful focus.

A deliberate breath consists of a slow, full, diaphragmatic (belly) inhale through the nose, finishing with a slower exhale through the mouth. It can be used when the person notices they have lost composure and focus to restore presence.

Such breathing can also be a full-time endeavor. Twenty-four/seven deliberate breathing can establish continuous calm composure and focus. Slow, rhythmic breathing physiologically cools the nervous system and vastly improves focus, according to the research reported in the book Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art (Nestor, 2020).

The Yeager Voice

Test-pilot Chuck Yeager and the Bell X-1 Glamorous Glennis,
Source: United States Air Force / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

"Calm is contagious"

That’s a core leadership principle of the Navy SEALs and those trained in other specialized military forces. People under stress require leaders who stay composed under pressured circumstances. That keeps them calm and composed so they can effectively do their job. That applies to athletes as well as military personnel.

Relating to all that is "the Yeager voice," a phrase coined in honor of famed test pilot Chuck Yeager, renowned for his calm, slow-speaking manner during high-stress aviation scenarios. He was the first pilot to break the sound barrier in 1947, flying at 700 mph.

You may have noticed such a voice when listening to a commercial airline pilot speaking to passengers when conditions of air turbulence and other dangerous conditions emerge. Speaking with a composed, slow cadence during stressful circumstances exudes reassuring control and competence of the pilot and will calm all onboard.

Humans tend to mirror each other’s emotional state. Yelling at someone, especially under difficult circumstances, will only make them more upset and disrupt their focus. When we stay composed, it calms the people we're with. It’s called co-regulation.

Take note, everybody. Yelling and screaming after someone makes a mistake or amid conversations will only escalate things into total emotional and behavioral chaos. When athletes mess up, nobody feels worse than they do. They need a Yeager voice to assist in rebooting themselves to regain composure and presence, thus enabling them to do their job.

Deliberate (tactical) breathing enables the ability to pivot out of intense emotions and use a Yeager voice to keep things from escalating into impulsive outbursts that can disrupt optimal performance and constructive discussions, and most importantly, damage relationships.

Instead of temper tantrums, try a Yeager voice. If it works under military conditions, it just might work in an athletic, school, and home setting.

OODA Loop

Another military skill requiring deliberate (tactical) breathing is this process, developed by U.S. Air Force Colonel John Boyd in the early 1970s.

OODA is an acronym that represents the following:

  • Observe: Quickly gather internal and external data.
  • Orient: Analyze the data to make sense of it, correct errors of thinking, and put it all together. It’s like solving a puzzle.
  • Decide: Wisely select the choice that makes the most sense.
  • Act: Enact your decision. Test it out first, if time allows.
OODA Loop depicted, here, as an ongoing process for wise decision-making and to assess action effectiveness of those moves. It's a process closely aligned with Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT).
Source: H.C. Berkowitz / Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0

"Loop" infers that OODA is a continuous decision-making process, especially designed for stressful circumstances encountered in the military.

Football quarterbacking is a great example of the OODA-looping process. The QB must carefully observe surroundings, including receiver location, weather conditions, and pocket protection, and internal data, including the called play, thinking, emotional information, and bodily data, such as tiredness and arm soreness.

They then orient, placing the informational puzzle pieces together to formulate a decision without allowing impulsive thoughts and emotions to lead them to a heave downfield into quadruple coverage.

Finally, the quarterback acts. Scramble out of the pocket, throw a screen pass, fake a throw, run, etc. Quick, effective decisions and actions, precisely what OODA loops are for.

Closely aligned with this process is ACT. ACT trains exquisite noticing of internal and external data; the ability to carefully process sensory information and thoughts, emotions, and bodily input; and wisely choosing workable actions.

A process for effective decisions enables optimal performance in the military, sports, and everything in life.

Breathe deliberately, OODA loop, and use your Yeager voice!
